sentence: That\'s a different mechanism from the [Spanish imperfect\'s accent rule](/spanish-imperfect-endings/), where the -ía endings take a tilde in every single form because of a hiato (a stressed closed vowel, here í, next to an open vowel), not because of where the stress falls.
note: Target explicitly grounds every -ía imperfect tilde in hiatus, distinct from regular preterite final stress.
target_quote: 'Here every single form carries a written accent, on the í, and that\'s a different rule from the one that puts the accent on hablábamos. Real Academia Española\'s orthography guide states that a stressed closed vowel (i or u) next to an open vowel (a, e, o) always takes a written accent, overriding the general stress rules entirely, and lists sabíais, an imperfect form, as one of its own examples of the rule. That combination, a stressed í touching an a, is called a hiato: without the accent, ia would tend to collapse into a single glide syllable, and the accent is what keeps the í as its own syllable and marks it as the stressed one. Every person of the -ía set has that same í-next-to-a shape, which is why the accent shows up in all six forms instead of just one.',
